# Introduction

This section introduces the project, its dataset, and the questions guiding the analyses. 

::: panel-tabset

## Background and Relevance
Student life is often the first time when people start living alone and organizing life themselves. With new environments and new responsibilities come new challenges. Therefore, we deem it necessary to assess the connections of student habits, performance, and mental wellbeing in order to set some stepping stones for further investigations into ideal student life balances.

## Dataset
The Dataset was found on  [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mdismielhossenabir/psychosocial-dimensions-of-student-life)
and published by Md. Ismiel Hossen Abier. It is titled
*Psychosocial Dimensions of Student Life*.

The extracted code can be found through zenodo, and extracted via the r code below.
```{r}
#| output: false
read.csv("https://zenodo.org/records/10573715/files/CSE_student_performances%20%281%29.csv")
```

The sample consists of 99 computer science students who self-reported a number of social and mental health variables.

## Overview and Research Questions
Our project first outlines some demographic student variables in order to provide a contextual frame for interpreting this data.
Then, self-reported habits and the students' performance are mapped onto each other.

There are two main section of analyses completed.

1. **Sleep and Mental Wellbeing**

   In which the sample's sleep duration (in hours) and Depression status are demonstrated by asking the following questions.

   - How much do students sleep?
   - How do students report their depression status?

   **RQ1:** Is daily sleep duration associated with self-reported academic performance among students?

   - **Hypotheses:**
     - H₀: Sleep duration does not differ systematically across the four academic performance groups.
     - H₁: Sleep duration differs across at least two academic performance groups.

   **RQ2:** Is daily sleep duration associated with self-reported depression status among students?

   - **Hypotheses:**
     - H₀: Sleep duration does not differ systematically between the depression-status groups.
     - H₁: Sleep duration differs across at least two depression-status groups.

2. **Students' Social Life**

   In which the following questions are answered based on analyses of students' self-report answers.

   - How many friends do students have?
   - Do students like giving presentations?
   - Do students like new things?

   Additionally, we mapped the relationships between the three social variables mentioned right above this.

   **RQ:** How do reported friendship counts differ across combinations of preferences for presentations and new things?

   - **Hypotheses:**
     - H₀: Students who like to both give presentations and new things will NOT have more friends than other students. 
     - H₁: Students who like to both give presentations and new things will have more friends than those who do not.

:::

## Loading data
Paste and run the following code to obtain the dataset and add it to the environment under the name "reports". This is important because it will be referred to as "reports" throughout the document.

## Loading data


```{r}
reports <- read.csv("https://zenodo.org/records/10573715/files/CSE_student_performances%20%281%29.csv")

# Error checks for the dataset

stopifnot(exists("reports"))

if (nrow(reports) == 0) {
  stop("Error: The dataset contains no rows.")
}

required_columns <- c(
  "SleepPerDayHours",
  "AcademicPerformance",
  "DepressionStatus",
  "Age",
  "Gender",
  "TakingNoteInClass",
  "FaceChallangesToCompleteAcademicTask",
  "LikePresentation",
  "SleepPerDayHours",
  "NumberOfFriend",
  "LikeNewThings"
)

missing_columns <- setdiff(
  required_columns,
  names(reports)
)

if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "Error: Missing columns:",
      paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}
```

## Student Profile

::: panel-tabset
### Student Age, visible by Gender

The following plot demonstrates the student ages within the sample.
The dropdown menu can be utilized to show the age distribution according to Gender (Male/Female).
The x-axis shows age, whereas the y-axis shows the number of students per age group.

```{r}
#| warning: false
age_data <- reports %>%
  filter(!is.na(Age), !is.na(Gender))

age_min <- floor(min(age_data$Age))
age_max <- ceiling(max(age_data$Age))
bin_size <- 1

mean_age <- mean(age_data$Age, na.rm = TRUE)
median_age <- median(age_data$Age, na.rm = TRUE)

# Assorting groups shown in the dropdown
groups <- c("All students", unique(as.character(age_data$Gender)))

# Creating one histogram trace per group
student_demo_plot <- plot_ly()

for (i in seq_along(groups)) {
  
  group_name <- groups[i]
  
  group_data <- if (group_name == "All students") {
    age_data
  } else {
    filter(age_data, as.character(Gender) == group_name)
  }
  
  student_demo_plot <- add_trace(
    student_demo_plot,
    data = group_data,
    x = ~Age,
    type = "histogram",
    name = group_name,
    visible = i == 1,
    opacity = 0.85,
    xbins = list(
      start = age_min,
      end = age_max + 1,
      size = bin_size
    ),
    marker = list(
      color = viridis(length(groups), option = "D")[i]
    ),
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "Age: %{x}",
      "<br>Students: %{y}",
      "<extra></extra>"
    )
  )
}

# Adding dropdown menu

# Each group has a histogram, mean line, and median line

# Calculate mean and median for each group
group_stats <- lapply(groups, function(group_name) {
  group_data <- if (group_name == "All students") {
    age_data
  } else {
    filter(age_data, as.character(Gender) == group_name)
  }

  list(
    mean = mean(group_data$Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(group_data$Age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
})

# Add mean and median lines for each group
for (i in seq_along(groups)) {
  student_demo_plot <- student_demo_plot %>%
    add_segments(
      x = group_stats[[i]]$mean,
      xend = group_stats[[i]]$mean,
      y = 0, yend = 1,
      yref = "paper",
      name = paste0(groups[i], " mean: ",
                    round(group_stats[[i]]$mean, 1)),
      line = list(color = "red", width = 2, dash = "dash"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      visible = i == 1,
      inherit = FALSE
    ) %>%
    add_segments(
      x = group_stats[[i]]$median,
      xend = group_stats[[i]]$median,
      y = 0, yend = 1,
      yref = "paper",
      name = paste0(groups[i], " median: ",
                    round(group_stats[[i]]$median, 1)),
      line = list(color = "blue", width = 2, dash = "dot"),
      showlegend = TRUE,
      visible = i == 1,
      inherit = FALSE
    )
}

# Set visibility for histogram and its matching indicator lines
num_groups <- length(groups)
total_traces <- num_groups * 3

dropdown_buttons <- lapply(seq_along(groups), function(i) {
  visible_traces <- rep(FALSE, total_traces)
  visible_traces[i] <- TRUE
  visible_traces[num_groups + 2 * i - 1] <- TRUE
  visible_traces[num_groups + 2 * i] <- TRUE

  list(
    method = "update",
    args = list(
      list(visible = visible_traces),
      list(title = paste("Age Distribution:", groups[i]))
    ),
    label = groups[i]
  )
})

# Setting plot details
student_demo_plot <- student_demo_plot %>%
  layout(
    title = "Age Distribution: All students",
    bargap = 0.2,
    margin = list(t = 100),
    template = "plotly_white",
    xaxis = list(title = "Age"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Number of students"),
    updatemenus = list(
      list(
        type = "dropdown",
        buttons = dropdown_buttons,
        x = 1,
        y = 1.18,
        xanchor = "right"
      )
    ),
    margin = list(t = 100)
  )

student_demo_plot
```
**Interpretation:** 
the histograms shows the overall distributions of Ages within the sample, and separated by two Gender categories. All students are between the ages of 20 and 26, with the mean being 22.5 for the entire sample, 22.7 for men, and 22.2 for women. The median is 23 for men and the overall student sample, but 22 for women: This shows that while men in this sample are slightly older on average, the difference between the two groups is not substantial.

### Gender Composition
This bar chart demonstrates the gender composition within our utilized sample. The different bars refer to students within separate gender categories, and the numbers as well as percentages of those within a bar can be read out on top of the bars or via the y-axis.

```{r}
### Gender Composition
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

# Summarise the gender composition
gender_data <- reports %>%
  filter(!is.na(Gender)) %>%
  mutate(Gender = trimws(as.character(Gender))) %>%
  count(Gender, name = "Students") %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Students / sum(Students),
    Label = paste0(
      Students, " (", round(Percentage, 1), "%)"
    )
  )

# Create the bar chart
ggplot(gender_data,
       aes(x = reorder(Gender, -Students),
           y = Students,
           fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = Label),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gender Composition of the Student Sample",
    subtitle = "Number and percentage of students in each category",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of students",
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
**Interpretation:** 
The gender composition plots highlight that the sample is relatively balanced, and not dominated by either Gender, although there are slightly more male participants.

## Study Habits
:::panel-tabset
### Academic Performance in relation to Taking Notes in Class: Dynamic Plot
Academic performance can be sorted by "Below average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent", and Taking Notes is quantified in "Yes", "No", and "Maybe" answer.
The animation can be started by pressing the "Play" button on the left. Alternatively, it is possible to look at all groups manually.

```{r}
# Counting number of students in each combination
habit_data <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(TakingNoteInClass),
    !is.na(AcademicPerformance)
  ) %>%
  count(AcademicPerformance, TakingNoteInClass, name = "Students") %>%
  group_by(AcademicPerformance) %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Students / sum(Students)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Preserve the original category order 
performance_levels <- unique(reports$AcademicPerformance)
habit_data$AcademicPerformance <- factor(
  habit_data$AcademicPerformance,
  levels = performance_levels
)

# Animate between performance categories
animated_figure <- plot_ly(
  data = habit_data,
  x = ~TakingNoteInClass,
  y = ~Percentage,
  frame = ~AcademicPerformance,
  type = "bar",
  color = ~TakingNoteInClass,
  text = ~paste0(round(Percentage, 1), "%"),
  textposition = "outside",
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Note-taking: %{x}",
    "<br>Percentage: %{y:.1f}%",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Note-taking Habits Across Academic Performance Groups",
    xaxis = list(title = "Do you take notes in class?"),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Percentage of Students (%)",
      range = c(0, 110)
    ),
    barmode = "group"
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(
    frame = 1000,
    transition = 500,
    redraw = TRUE
  ) %>%
  animation_button() %>%
  animation_slider()

animated_figure
```


```{r}

# Count students in each academic performance group
group_counts <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(AcademicPerformance),
    !is.na(TakingNoteInClass)
  ) %>%
  count(AcademicPerformance, name = "Number of students")

knitr::kable(
  group_counts,
  col.names = c("Academic Performance", "Number of Students"),
  caption = "Number of students included in the note-taking analysis"
)

```
**Interpretation:**
The chart indicates note taking habit differences among students within different academic performance groups. Most interestingly, 100% of students performing below average answer "yes" to taking notes in class, whereas no excellent students answer "yes" to note-taking. 
However, we added the table below to highlight careful interpretation of these results, because percentages are descriptive. Therefore, differences in group size may affect the observed results, wherefore we should not draw definite causality conclusions based on this.


### Depression Status and Academic Performance

Here we used a stacked bar chart to assess the amount of students per academic performance group within each depression-status category. The bars show the depression-status categories (No, Sometimes, Yes), and the colored contents show the different academic performance groups. Hovering over one of the colored segments will show the number and percentage of students within.
```{r}
depression_data <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(DepressionStatus),
    !is.na(AcademicPerformance)
  ) %>%
  count(
    DepressionStatus,
    AcademicPerformance,
    name = "Students"
  ) %>%
  group_by(DepressionStatus) %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Students / sum(Students)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

performance_categories <- unique(
  depression_data$AcademicPerformance
)

depression_plot <- plot_ly(
  data = depression_data,
  x = ~DepressionStatus,
  y = ~Percentage,
  color = ~AcademicPerformance,
  colors = viridis(
    length(performance_categories),
    option = "D"
  ),
  type = "bar",
  customdata = ~Students,
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Depression status: %{x}",
    "<br>Performance: %{fullData.name}",
    "<br>Students: %{customdata}",
    "<br>Percentage: %{y:.1f}%",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Academic Performance by Depression Status",
    xaxis = list(title = "Depression status"),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Percentage of students",
      range = c(0, 100)
    ),
    barmode = "stack",
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Academic performance")),
    template = "plotly_white"
  )

depression_plot

```
**Interpretation:**
The colored segments show that students whose self-reported performance is average, good, or excellent, are represented in all levels of depression to degrees that don't vary drastically. However, the four students performing below average have all indicated "yes" when asked about whether they experience depression. 

### Challenges in completing Academic Tasks

```{r}

  layout(
    title = "Challenges Completing Academic Tasks",
    xaxis = list(title = "Response"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Number of students"),
    template = "plotly_white",
    updatemenus = list(
      list(
        type = "buttons",
        direction = "right",
        x = 0,
        y = 1.18,
        buttons = list(
          list(
            label = "Counts",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = list(TRUE, FALSE)),
              list(yaxis = list(title = "Number of students"))
            )
          ),
          list(
            label = "Percentages",
            method = "update",

              list(visible = list(FALSE, TRUE)),

            )
          )
        )
      )
    ),
    margin = list(t = 100)

challenge_plot
```
**Interpretation:** 
The number of students option was incorporated in order to demonstrate how many students selected each answer possibility. The percentages option helps visualize the actual shares of responses. Whether challenges are experienced by students differs between students, but does not differ substantially between levels of challenge.

### Challenges in completing Academic tasks and performance

The above demonstrated academic task challenges plotted in relation to academic performance.

```{r}
performance_order <- c(
  "Below Average",
  "Average",
  "Good",
  "Excellent"
)

# Check the exact performance labels in your data
print(table(reports$AcademicPerformance, useNA = "ifany"))

challenge_data <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(FaceChallangesToCompleteAcademicTask),
    !is.na(AcademicPerformance)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    AcademicPerformance = trimws(
      as.character(AcademicPerformance)
    ),
    ChallengeResponse = trimws(
      as.character(FaceChallangesToCompleteAcademicTask)
    ),
    # Standardise case while matching the four categories
    PerformanceMatch = tolower(AcademicPerformance),
    PerformanceMatch = case_when(
      PerformanceMatch == "below average" ~ "Below Average",
      PerformanceMatch == "average" ~ "Average",
      PerformanceMatch == "good" ~ "Good",
      PerformanceMatch == "excellent" ~ "Excellent",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    AcademicPerformance = factor(
      PerformanceMatch,
      levels = performance_order,
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(AcademicPerformance)) %>%
  count(
    AcademicPerformance,
    ChallengeResponse,
    name = "Students"
  ) %>%
  complete(
    AcademicPerformance = factor(
      performance_order,
      levels = performance_order,
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    ChallengeResponse,
    fill = list(Students = 0)
  ) %>%
  group_by(AcademicPerformance) %>%
  mutate(
    GroupTotal = sum(Students),
    Percentage = if_else(
      GroupTotal > 0,
      100 * Students / GroupTotal,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

challenge_levels <- unique(challenge_data$ChallengeResponse)

challenge_colors <- setNames(
  viridis(length(challenge_levels), option = "D"),
  challenge_levels
)

plot_ly(
  data = challenge_data,
  x = ~AcademicPerformance,
  y = ~Percentage,
  color = ~ChallengeResponse,
  colors = challenge_colors,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  customdata = ~Students,
  connectgaps = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "Performance: %{x}",
    "<br>Challenge response: %{fullData.name}",
    "<br>Percentage: %{y:.1f}%",
    "<br>Students: %{customdata}",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Academic Task Challenges Across Performance Levels"
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Academic Performance",
      type = "category",
      categoryorder = "array",
      categoryarray = performance_order
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Percentage Within Performance Group",
      ticksuffix = "%",
      range = c(0, 100)
    ),
    template = "plotly_white",
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Challenge response")),
    margin = list(t = 80, b = 80)
  )


```
**Interpretation:** 
This plot shows how level of challenge experienced differs across academic performance categories. Interestingly, all students performing below average experience challenges most the time. In contrast, none of the excellent performing students indicated any experienced challenges. These two categories show the biggest difference within the sample, whereas the difference in experienced challenges between students indicating "average" or "good" is not as severe, although present, and also showing the pattern that with increasing performance we see decreasing challenges experienced.

:::

# Analysis 1 - Sleep and Mental Well being

Sleep is an important part of student life and may be related to both academic performance and mental well-being. In this part of the analysis, we explore students' daily sleep duration and examine whether sleep patterns differ across academic performance and self-reported depression-status groups. We begin by looking at the overall distributions, before exploring differences between the groups.

::: panel-tabset
## Distribution of Daily Sleep Hours

### How much do students sleep?

We first examined daily sleep duration among the 99 students. The summary statistics describe typical sleep duration and its variability, while the histogram shows how sleep hours are distributed across the sample.

```{r}
#descriptive statistics for sleep duration

sleep_summary <- reports %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = mean(SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = min(SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = max(SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Mean = round(Mean, 2),
    Median = round(Median, 2),
    SD = round(SD, 2)
  )

#display formatted summary table

knitr::kable(
  sleep_summary,
  caption = "Summary statistics for daily sleep duration (hours)",
  align = "c"
)

#distribution of daily sleep hours

ggplot(reports, aes(x = SleepPerDayHours)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    boundary = 3.5,
    fill = "#21918C",  #Viridis teal
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(reports$SleepPerDayHours, na.rm = TRUE),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#440154",  #Dark Viridis purple
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
  title = "Daily sleep duration among students",
  subtitle = "The dashed line indicates the median",
  x = "Hours of sleep per day",
  y = "Number of students",
  caption = "Source: Psychosocial Dimensions of Student Life dataset"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 4:12) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

### What does the distribution show?

The histogram shows that reported sleep duration was concentrated between 4 and 8 hours per day, with 8 hours being the most frequently observed value. Relatively few students reported sleeping 10 or 12 hours. Although sleep duration varied across the sample, most students reported sleep durations within this 4–8-hour range.

## Distribution of self-reported depression status

### How do students report their depression status?

Before examining whether sleep duration differs across depression-status groups, we first explored how students described their own depression status. The interactive chart below shows the number and percentage of students in each category. Use the buttons to switch between counts and percentages.

```{r}
#frequency analysis and visualisation of depression status

depression_summary <- reports %>%
  filter(!is.na(DepressionStatus)) %>%
  mutate(DepressionStatus = trimws(as.character(DepressionStatus))) %>%
  count(DepressionStatus, name = "Frequency") %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = Frequency / sum(Frequency) * 100,
    Label = paste0(
      Frequency, " (", round(Percentage, 1), "%)"
    )
  )

#interactive depression-status chart
#users can switch between counts and percentages

depression_plot <- plot_ly(
  data = depression_summary,
  x = ~Frequency,
  y = ~reorder(DepressionStatus, Frequency),
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  name = "Number of students",
  marker = list(
    color = c("#440154", "#21918C", "#FDE725")
  ),
  text = ~paste0(Frequency, " students"),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "<b>%{y}</b>",
    "<br>Number of students: %{x}",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  visible = TRUE
) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = depression_summary,
    x = ~Percentage,
    y = ~reorder(DepressionStatus, Frequency),
    type = "bar",
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Percentage",
    marker = list(
      color = c("#440154", "#21918C", "#FDE725")
    ),
    text = ~paste0(round(Percentage, 1), "%"),
    hovertemplate = paste(
      "<b>%{y}</b>",
      "<br>Percentage: %{x:.1f}%",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Self-reported depression status among students"
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Number of students",
      rangemode = "tozero"
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "",
      categoryorder = "trace"
    ),
    barmode = "overlay",
    updatemenus = list(
      list(
        type = "buttons",
        direction = "right",
        x = 0,
        y = 1.15,
        buttons = list(
          list(
            label = "Counts",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = list(TRUE, FALSE)),
              list(
                "xaxis.title" = "Number of students"
              )
            )
          ),
          list(
            label = "Percentages",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = list(FALSE, TRUE)),
              list(
                "xaxis.title" = "Percentage of students (%)"
              )
            )
          )
        )
      )
    ),
    margin = list(l = 100, t = 110),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

depression_plot
```

### What does the distribution show?

The most common response was "Sometimes", reported by 44 students (44.4%). A further 34 students (34.3%) selected "Yes", while 21 students (21.2%) selected "No". Thus, most students reported experiencing depression sometimes or answered yes to the depression-status question, while around one-fifth selected no.

These responses describe students' self-reported depression status and should not be interpreted as clinical diagnoses. In the next part of the analysis, we examine whether reported sleep duration differs across these three groups.

## Sleep duration across academic performance groups

### Does sleep duration differ across academic performance groups?

We next examined whether daily sleep duration varied according to students' self-reported academic performance. The dot plot below shows individual students' reported sleep duration, with a black diamond marking the median for each group. This allows us to compare both the typical sleep duration and the variation within each group.

**Research question:** Is daily sleep duration associated with self-reported academic performance among students?

- **H₀:** Sleep duration does not differ systematically across the four academic performance groups.
- **H₁:** Sleep duration differs across at least two academic performance groups.

```{r}
#comparing individual sleep durations across performance groups

sleep_performance <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(SleepPerDayHours),
    !is.na(AcademicPerformance)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    AcademicPerformance = factor(
      AcademicPerformance,
      levels = c("Below average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent")
    ),
    PerformancePosition = as.numeric(AcademicPerformance)
  )

#calculate group medians and sample sizes

sleep_group_summary <- sleep_performance %>%
  group_by(AcademicPerformance, PerformancePosition) %>%
  summarise(
    MedianSleep = median(SleepPerDayHours),
    N = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#add slight horizontal jitter so overlapping observations are visible

set.seed(123)

sleep_performance <- sleep_performance %>%
  mutate(
    JitteredPosition = PerformancePosition +
      runif(n(), -0.12, 0.12)
  )

#interactive dot plot

plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sleep_performance,
    x = ~JitteredPosition,
    y = ~SleepPerDayHours,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    color = ~AcademicPerformance,
    colors = c("#440154", "#31688E", "#35B779", "#FDE725"),
    marker = list(size = 9, opacity = 0.7),
    text = ~paste0(
      "Performance: ", AcademicPerformance,
      "<br>Sleep: ", SleepPerDayHours, " hours"
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "Individual students"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sleep_group_summary,
    x = ~PerformancePosition,
    y = ~MedianSleep,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    marker = list(
      symbol = "diamond",
      size = 15,
      color = "black",
      line = list(color = "white", width = 1)
    ),
    text = ~paste0(
      "Performance: ", AcademicPerformance,
      "<br>Median sleep: ", MedianSleep, " hours",
      "<br>Number of students: ", N
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "Group median"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Sleep duration across academic performance groups"
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Academic performance",
      tickmode = "array",
      tickvals = 1:4,
      ticktext = c(
        "Below average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent"
      ),
      range = c(0.5, 4.5)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Hours of sleep per day",
      dtick = 1
    ),
    margin = list(b = 90, t = 80),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2)
  )

```

### What patterns can we observe?

The group medians suggest differences in typical sleep duration across academic performance groups. Students in the *Below average* group reported a median of 5 hours, compared with 7 hours in the *Average* group, 6 hours in the *Good* group, and 8 hours in the *Excellent* group.

However, the group sizes are unequal, particularly for the *Below average* group (n = 4) and the *Excellent* group (n = 9). These descriptive differences therefore need to be considered alongside the statistical tests.

### Statistical analysis: Is the overall difference significant?

Because sleep duration is compared across four independent groups, we used a Kruskal–Wallis test to examine whether sleep duration differed across the academic performance groups.

```{r}
#Kruskal-Wallis test to compare sleep duration across performance groups
sleep_test <- kruskal.test(
  SleepPerDayHours ~ AcademicPerformance,
  data = sleep_performance
)

sleep_test

```

The Kruskal–Wallis test indicated a statistically significant difference in sleep duration across the four academic performance groups, χ²(3) = 13.30, *p* = .004. We therefore reject the null hypothesis that sleep duration does not differ systematically across the groups.

However, this overall result does not tell us which specific groups differ. We therefore conducted pairwise comparisons to investigate these differences further.

### Which groups differ?

We used Dunn's post-hoc tests with a Holm correction to account for multiple comparisons.

```{r}
#pairwise comparisons between academic performance groups
dunn_results <- rstatix::dunn_test(
  data = sleep_performance,
  SleepPerDayHours ~ AcademicPerformance,
  p.adjust.method = "holm"
) %>%
  mutate(
    statistic = round(statistic, 2),
    p = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    p.adj = format.pval(p.adj, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  ) %>%
  select(
    group1, group2, n1, n2, statistic, p, p.adj, p.adj.signif
  )

knitr::kable(
  dunn_results,
  col.names = c(
    "Group 1", "Group 2", "N₁", "N₂",
    "Test statistic", "Unadjusted p", "Holm-adjusted p", "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "Pairwise Dunn tests comparing sleep duration across academic performance groups",
  align = "llrrrlll"
)
```

Holm-adjusted Dunn tests indicated significant differences in sleep duration between the *Below average* and *Excellent* performance groups (p = .028), and between the *Good* and *Excellent* groups (p = .048). The other pairwise comparisons were not statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that sleep duration differed between some, but not all, academic performance groups. However, the small sample sizes in the *Below average* (n = 4) and *Excellent* (n = 9) groups warrant caution when interpreting these differences.

Thus, the overall difference appears to be driven partly by differences involving the *Excellent* group. However, the small sample sizes in the *Below average* and *Excellent* groups mean these comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

### How large is the observed difference?

To complement the significance tests, we estimated epsilon-squared (ε²) as an effect-size measure for the Kruskal–Wallis test.

```{r}
#calculate effect size
H <- as.numeric(sleep_test$statistic)
k <- nlevels(droplevels(sleep_performance$AcademicPerformance))
n <- nrow(sleep_performance)

epsilon_squared <- max(0, (H - k + 1) / (n - k))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = "Epsilon-squared (ε²)",
    Estimate = round(epsilon_squared, 3)
  ),
  caption = "Estimated effect size for the Kruskal–Wallis test",
  align = "lc"
)
```

The estimated epsilon-squared was ε² = 0.108, suggesting a non-negligible difference in sleep-duration distributions across academic performance groups. This estimate should be interpreted cautiously because effect-size conventions vary and the groups are small and unequal.

### What do these findings tell us?

Overall, sleep duration differed across academic performance groups, with the *Excellent* group reporting the highest median sleep duration. The post-hoc comparisons showed significant differences between this group and both the *Below average* and *Good* groups, but not between all groups.

These findings indicate an association between sleep duration and self-reported academic performance in this sample. However, the analysis cannot establish that sleeping longer leads to better academic performance, and the small sizes of some groups limit the certainty of the pairwise findings. We next examine whether sleep duration also differs across students' self-reported depression-status groups.

## Sleep duration across self-reported depression-status groups

### Does sleep duration differ across depression-status groups?

After examining academic performance, we turned to students' self-reported depression status. We explored whether daily sleep duration varied between students who answered "No", "Sometimes", or "Yes". The summary statistics and dot plot below allow us to compare typical sleep duration and the variation within each group.

**Research question:** Is daily sleep duration associated with self-reported depression status among students?

- **H₀:** Sleep duration does not differ systematically between the depression-status groups.
- **H₁:** Sleep duration differs across at least two depression-status groups.

```{r}
#prepare data for the sleep and well-being analysis
sleep_wellbeing <- reports %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(SleepPerDayHours),
    !is.na(DepressionStatus)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    DepressionStatus = factor(
      trimws(as.character(DepressionStatus)),
      levels = c("No", "Sometimes", "Yes")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(DepressionStatus))

#summarise sleep duration by depression status
wellbeing_descriptives <- sleep_wellbeing %>%
  group_by(DepressionStatus) %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    MedianSleep = median(SleepPerDayHours),
    IQR = IQR(SleepPerDayHours),
    MeanSleep = mean(SleepPerDayHours),
    SD = sd(SleepPerDayHours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    MeanSleep = round(MeanSleep, 2),
    SD = round(SD, 2)
  )

knitr::kable(
  wellbeing_descriptives,
  col.names = c(
    "Depression status", "N", "Median (hours)",
    "IQR", "Mean (hours)", "SD"
  ),
  caption = "Summary statistics for sleep duration by depression status",
  align = "lrrrrr"
)
```

```{r}
#calculate group medians and sample sizes

wellbeing_summary <- sleep_wellbeing %>%
  group_by(DepressionStatus) %>%
  summarise(
    MedianSleep = median(SleepPerDayHours),
    N = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    GroupPosition = as.numeric(DepressionStatus)
  )

  
  #add slight horizontal jitter to separate overlapping points

set.seed(123)

sleep_wellbeing <- sleep_wellbeing %>%
  mutate(
    GroupPosition = as.numeric(DepressionStatus),
    JitteredPosition = GroupPosition + runif(n(), -0.12, 0.12)
  )
  
  #interactive dot plot
  
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sleep_wellbeing,
    x = ~JitteredPosition,
    y = ~SleepPerDayHours,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    color = ~DepressionStatus,
    colors = c("#440154", "#21918C", "#FDE725"),
    marker = list(size = 9, opacity = 0.7),
    text = ~paste0(
      "Depression status: ", DepressionStatus,
      "<br>Sleep duration: ", SleepPerDayHours, " hours"
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "Individual students"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = wellbeing_summary,
    x = ~GroupPosition,
    y = ~MedianSleep,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    marker = list(
      symbol = "diamond",
      size = 15,
      color = "black",
      line = list(color = "white", width = 1)
    ),
    text = ~paste0(
      "Depression status: ", DepressionStatus,
      "<br>Median sleep: ", MedianSleep, " hours",
      "<br>Number of students: ", N
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "Group median"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Sleep duration across depression-status groups"
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Self-reported depression status",
      tickmode = "array",
      tickvals = 1:3,
      ticktext = c("No", "Sometimes", "Yes"),
      range = c(0.5, 3.5)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Hours of sleep per day",
      dtick = 1
    ),
    margin = list(b = 90, t = 80),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2)
  )
```

### What patterns can we observe?

The dot plot shows individual students' reported sleep duration, with black diamonds indicating the median for each group. Students who answered "No" generally reported more sleep, with a median of 8 hours per day. This decreased to 7 hours among students who answered "Sometimes" and 5 hours among those who answered "Yes".

The individual observations also show variation within each group, with some students reporting considerably more or less sleep than their group's median. Nevertheless, the overall pattern suggests that lower reported sleep duration tended to coincide with reporting depression more frequently.

These are descriptive patterns only; we next use statistical tests to determine whether the observed differences between groups are statistically significant.

### Statistical analysis: Is the overall difference significant?

We used a Kruskal–Wallis test to examine whether sleep duration differed across the three independent depression-status groups.

```{r}
#test whether sleep duration differs across depression-status groups
wellbeing_test <- kruskal.test(
  SleepPerDayHours ~ DepressionStatus,
  data = sleep_wellbeing
)

wellbeing_test
```

The Kruskal–Wallis test indicated a statistically significant difference in sleep duration across the depression-status groups, χ²(2) = 23.41, *p* \< .001. We therefore reject the null hypothesis that sleep duration does not differ systematically between the groups.

However, the overall test does not identify which groups differ from one another. We therefore conducted pairwise comparisons to investigate these differences further.

### Which groups differ?

We used Dunn's post-hoc tests with a Holm correction to account for multiple comparisons.

```{r}
#pairwise comparisons with Holm correction
wellbeing_pairwise <- rstatix::dunn_test(
  data = sleep_wellbeing,
  SleepPerDayHours ~ DepressionStatus,
  p.adjust.method = "holm"
)

wellbeing_results_table <- wellbeing_pairwise %>%
  mutate(
    statistic = round(statistic, 2),
    p = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
    p.adj = format.pval(p.adj, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  ) %>%
  select(
    group1, group2, n1, n2, statistic, p, p.adj
  )

knitr::kable(
  wellbeing_results_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Group 1", "Group 2", "N₁", "N₂",
    "Test statistic", "Unadjusted p", "Holm-adjusted p"
  ),
  caption = "Pairwise Dunn tests comparing sleep duration across depression-status groups",
  align = "llrrrll"
)
```

All three pairwise comparisons were statistically significant after the Holm correction. Sleep duration differed between the "No" and "Sometimes" groups (*p* = .028), the "No" and "Yes" groups (*p* \< .001), and the "Sometimes" and "Yes" groups (*p* = .003).

Together with the descriptive statistics, these findings suggest that reported sleep duration was lower in groups reporting depression more frequently. The largest difference in median sleep duration was between the "No" group (8 hours) and the "Yes" group (5 hours).

### How large is the observed difference?

To complement the significance tests, we estimated epsilon-squared (ε²) as an effect-size measure for the Kruskal–Wallis test.

```{r}
#calculate approximate epsilon-squared
H <- as.numeric(wellbeing_test$statistic)
k <- nlevels(droplevels(sleep_wellbeing$DepressionStatus))
n <- nrow(sleep_wellbeing)

epsilon_squared_wellbeing <- max(
  0, (H - k + 1) / (n - k)
)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = "Epsilon-squared (ε²)",
    Estimate = round(epsilon_squared_wellbeing, 3)
  ),
  caption = "Estimated effect size for the Kruskal–Wallis test",
  align = "lc"
)
```

The estimated epsilon-squared was ε² = 0.223, suggesting a notable difference in sleep-duration distributions across the depression-status groups. This complements the significant overall test, although the estimate should be interpreted as approximate.

### What do these findings tell us?

Overall, sleep duration differed across all three self-reported depression-status groups. Students who answered "No" reported the highest median sleep duration, those who answered "Sometimes" reported an intermediate median, and those who answered "Yes" reported the lowest median. The pairwise comparisons supported differences between every pair of groups.

These findings indicate an association between sleep duration and self-reported depression status in this sample. However, the data cannot establish a causal relationship or determine whether sleep duration influences depression status, depression status influences sleep, or other factors contribute to both. Furthermore, self-reported depression status should not be interpreted as a clinical diagnosis.
:::

# Analysis 2 - Student's social life

Another crucial part of student's life is their social relations and skills. Whether they have social connections they can rely on and how they see/deal with the social world directly affects not only their academic performance but life as whole. In this part we analyse the distribution of data in the relevant variables, how they relate to one another, and finally, we create a new variable related to social life based on the other relevant variables.

::: panel-tabset
## Number of friends

### **How many friends do students have?**

We examined students’ self-reported number of friends as an indicator of social network size. Of the 99 students, 95 provided a valid response and four had missing responses. The summary statistics describe the centre, variability, and range of reported counts.

```{r}
#descriptive statistics summary of variable friends data 
friend_summary <- reports %>%
  summarise(
    total_students = n(),
    valid_responses = sum(!is.na(NumberOfFriend)),
    missing_responses = sum(is.na(NumberOfFriend)),
    missing_percent = 100 * mean(is.na(NumberOfFriend)),
    mean_friends = mean(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_friends = sd(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_friends = median(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_friends = IQR(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum_friends = min(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum_friends = max(NumberOfFriend, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) 

#putting results in a more readable table
friend_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Statistic",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Statistic = gsub("_", " ", Statistic),
    Value = round(Value, 2)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Statistic", "Value"),
    caption = "Summary of statistics for number of friends"
  )

#plotting of distribution of number of friends
gghistostats(
  data = reports,
  x = NumberOfFriend,
  xlab = "Number of friends",
  title = "How many friends do students have on average?",
  subtitle = "Distribution of number of friends",
  binwidth = 3,
  centrality.type = "mean",
  centrality.line.args = list(
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ),
  bin.args = list(
    fill = viridisLite::viridis(5)[3],
    color = "white"
  ),
  results.subtitle = FALSE,               
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_bw()        
)
```

### **What does the distribution show?**

Friendship counts were strongly right-skewed, most students reported relatively few friends, while a small number reported much higher counts, reaching 100. The mean was 16.19 friends, compared with a median of 6 and an interquartile range of 12. The difference between the mean and median reflects the influence of high counts, making the median a useful description of a typical response.

## Liking presentations

### **Do students like giving presentations**

We examined whether students reported liking giving presentations. Although not a direct measure of social skills, presentation preference may be relevant to participation in some social situations

Because counts and percentages are already presented in the graph, a separate table was not included to avoid repeating the same information.

```{r}
#| warning: false

#preparing data to be plotted
presentation_counts <- reports %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(LikePresentation) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n),
    label = paste0(
      "n = ", n, " (",
      scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 1), ")"
    ),
    tooltip = paste0(
      "Response: ", LikePresentation,
      "<br>Students: ", n,
      "<br>Percentage: ",
      scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

#plotting distribution
plotly::ggplotly(
  ggplot(
    presentation_counts,
    aes(
      x = proportion,
      y = factor(LikePresentation),
      fill = factor(LikePresentation),
      text = tooltip
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(width = 0.6) +
    geom_label(
      aes(x = proportion / 2, label = label),
      fill = "white",
      colour = "black"
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    scale_x_continuous(
      labels = scales::label_percent(),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
      limits = c(0, 1)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Do students like giving public presentations?",
      subtitle = "Distribution of students' reported preferences",
      x = "Percentage of students",
      y = NULL,
      caption = paste("Total responses:", sum(presentation_counts$n))
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none"),
  tooltip = "text"
)

```

### What does the distribution show?

Among the 99 students examined, 69 (approximately 70%) reported liking giving presentations and 30 (approximately 30%) did not. Thus, liking presentations was more common than not liking presentations in this sample.

## Liking new things

### **Do students like new things?**

We also examined whether students reported liking new things. This question captures a general preference for novelty, while also not a validated measure of social skills, it could also be relevant to participation in certain social situations. We included it to explore whether this preference was associated with friendship counts.

Because counts and percentages are already presented in the graph, a separate table was not included to avoid repeating the same information.

```{r}
#| warning: false

#preparing data to be plotted
new_things_counts <- reports %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(LikeNewThings) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n),
    label = paste0(
      "n = ", n, " (",
      scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 1), ")"
    ),
    tooltip = paste0(
      "Response: ", LikeNewThings,
      "<br>Students: ", n,
      "<br>Percentage: ",
      scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

#ploting data distribution
plotly::ggplotly(
  ggplot(
    new_things_counts,
    aes(
      x = proportion,
      y = factor(LikeNewThings),
      fill = factor(LikeNewThings),
      text = tooltip
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(width = 0.6) +
    geom_label(
      aes(x = proportion / 2, label = label),
      fill = "white",
      colour = "black"
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D") +
    scale_x_continuous(
      labels = scales::label_percent(),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
      limits = c(0, 1)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "How students feel about new things",
      subtitle = "Distribution of students' reported preferences",
      x = "Percentage of students",
      y = NULL,
      caption = paste("Total responses:", sum(new_things_counts$n))
    ) +

)
```

### What does this distribution show?

Among the 99 students, 89 (approximately 90%) reported liking new things and 10 (approximately 10%) did not. Similarly to liking to give presentations, liking new things was also more common than not liking new things in this sample.

## Relationship between social variables

### **RQ: How do reported friendship counts differ across combinations of preferences for presentations and new things?**

We explored whether students’ preferences for giving presentations and new things were associated with their reported number of friends. These preferences may relate to participation in activities that offer opportunities for social contact. Comparing friendship counts across the four preference combinations allows us to examine whether students with different combinations report different social network sizes.

- **H₀:** Students who like to both give presentations and new things will NOT have more friends than other students. 

- **H₁:** Students who like to both give presentations and new things will have more friends than those who do not.

```{r}
#| warning: false

#preparing data to be analyzed
social_life_data <- reports %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  drop_na(NumberOfFriend) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(LikeNewThings, LikePresentation),
      ~ factor(.x, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
    ),
    preference_group = interaction(
      LikeNewThings,
      LikePresentation,
      sep = " / ",
      lex.order = TRUE,
      drop = TRUE
    )
  )

#getting group statistics
group_summary <- social_life_data %>%
  group_by(preference_group) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_friends = median(NumberOfFriend),
    iqr_friends = IQR(NumberOfFriend),
    mean_friends = mean(NumberOfFriend),
    sd_friends = sd(NumberOfFriend),
    minimum_friends = min(NumberOfFriend),
    maximum_friends = max(NumberOfFriend),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) 

#putting group summary results in a more readable table
group_summary %>%
  transmute(
    preference_group,
    n,
    median_friends,
    iqr_friends,
    mean_friends,
    sd_friends,
    range = str_c(minimum_friends, "–", maximum_friends)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Reported friendship counts by preference combination",
    col.names = c(
      "New things / Presentations",
      "Students",
      "Median",
      "IQR",
      "Mean",
      "SD",
      "Range"
    ),
    digits = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 0),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
  )

#plotting data
set.seed(11)

ggplotly(
  ggplot(
    social_life_data,
    aes(x = preference_group, y = NumberOfFriend)
  ) +
    geom_boxplot(
      width = 0.5,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      fill = "grey95"
    ) +
    geom_jitter(
      aes(
        colour = preference_group,
        text = str_c(
          "Likes new things: ", LikeNewThings,
          "<br>Likes presentations: ", LikePresentation,
          "<br>Number of friends: ", NumberOfFriend
        )
      ),
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      alpha = 0.7,
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D") +
    labs(
      title = "Number of friends by preferences",
      subtitle = "Group labels: likes new things / likes presentations",
      x = "Preference combination",
      y = "Number of friends",
      caption = paste(
        "Students with valid friendship counts:",
        nrow(social_life_data)
      )
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none"),
  tooltip = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    dragmode = "zoom",
    hovermode = "closest"
  ) %>%
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    displayModeBar = TRUE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = "reset"
  )

#running overall staistical comparison
kruskal_results <- social_life_data %>%
  kruskal_test(NumberOfFriend ~ preference_group) 

#putting statitcal comparison results in a more readable table
kruskal_results %>%
  transmute(
    test = "Kruskal–Wallis",
    n,
    statistic,
    df,
    p
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Overall comparison of friendship-count distributions",
    col.names = c("Test", "Students", "H", "df", "p-value"),
    digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0, 3),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
  )
```

Friendship counts showed no consistent increase across preference combinations (new things / presentations). Students who liked both had the widest spread, with several counts reaching 100, although their median was only 4. The median was higher among students who liked new things but disliked presentations (8.5), while students who disliked both had the lowest median (2). All four students who disliked new things but liked presentations reported 9 friends, so their box collapsed to a horizontal line. Despite these descriptive differences, the Kruskal–Wallis test did not provide clear evidence of differences in friendship-count distributions across groups, H(3)=4.26, p=.234. Therefore, although the graph may indicate some group differences, the statistical test provides evidence for the null hypothesis. Interpretation should be cautious because group sizes were small and unequal.

## Social variables and Academic performance

### **RQ: Are friendship counts and preferences for presentations and new things associated with higher self-reported academic performance?**

This research question explores whether students’ social connections and preferences for presenting and trying new things are related to how they rate their academic performance

- **H₀:** Friendship counts and preferences for presentations and new things are not associated with self-reported academic performance.

- **H₁:** Students with more friends and who like presentations and new things will tend to report higher academic performance.

```{r}
#preparing data to plot
academic_data <- reports %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename_with(trimws) %>%
  mutate(
    AcademicPerformance = factor(
      str_to_title(str_trim(as.character(AcademicPerformance))),
      levels = c("Below Average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  drop_na(NumberOfFriend)

#plotting data
set.seed(11)

academic_data %>%
  transmute(
    `Academic performance` = AcademicPerformance,
    `Number of friends` = NumberOfFriend
  ) %>%
  {ggplotly(
    ggplot(., aes(x = `Academic performance`, y = `Number of friends`)) +
      geom_boxplot(
        width = 0.5,
        outlier.shape = NA,
        fill = "grey95"
      ) +
      geom_jitter(
        aes(colour = `Academic performance`),
        width = 0.12,
        height = 0,
        alpha = 0.7,
        size = 2
      ) +
      scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D", drop = FALSE) +
      scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
      labs(
        title = "Friendship counts by academic performance",
        x = "Academic performance",
        y = "Number of friends"
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      theme(legend.position = "none"),
    tooltip = c("x", "y")
  )} %>%
  layout(dragmode = "zoom", hovermode = "closest") %>%
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    displayModeBar = TRUE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = "reset"
  )

#running statistical tests + putting it in a nice table
academic_data %>%
  {
    cor.test(
      x = .$NumberOfFriend,
      y = as.integer(.$AcademicPerformance),
      method = "spearman",
      exact = FALSE,
      alternative = "two.sided"
    )
  } %>%
  {
    tibble(
      test = "Spearman's rank correlation",
      n = nrow(academic_data),
      rho = unname(.$estimate),
      p = .$p.value
    )
  } %>%
  mutate(
    p = if_else(p < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Association between friendship count and academic performance",
    col.names = c("Test", "Students", "Spearman's rho", "p-value"),
    digits = c(0, 0, 3, 0),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
  )

```

The boxplot shows that reported friendship counts generally increase with academic performance. All four Below Average students reported one friend, while the Average and Good groups had higher medians and overlapping distributions. The Excellent group had the highest median, but also substantial variation, with friendship counts ranging from 3 to 80.

Among the 95 students analysed, Spearman’s rank correlation indicated a weak positive association between friendship count and academic performance (ρ = .282, p = .006). This association was statistically significant at the conventional .05 level, suggesting that students reporting more friends tended to report higher academic performance, supporting our hypothesis albeit weakly. However, the relationship was modest and does not establish that having more friends causes better academic perf

### Liking presentations

```{r}
#preparing data
presentation_academic <- reports %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename_with(trimws) %>%
  mutate(
    LikePresentation = factor(LikePresentation, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    AcademicPerformance = factor(
      str_to_title(str_trim(as.character(AcademicPerformance))),
      levels = c("Below Average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

#plotting (and bit of data preparation too)
presentation_academic %>%
  count(LikePresentation, AcademicPerformance) %>%
  group_by(LikePresentation) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n),
    hover = str_c(
      "Likes presentations: ", LikePresentation,
      "<br>Academic performance: ", AcademicPerformance,
      "<br>Students: ", n, " of ", sum(n),
      "<br>Percentage: ", scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  plot_ly(
    x = ~LikePresentation, y = ~proportion,
    color = ~AcademicPerformance,
    colors = viridisLite::viridis(4),
    type = "bar", text = ~hover, hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
 layout(
    title = "Academic performance by presentation preference",
    barmode = "stack",
    xaxis = list(title = "Likes giving presentations"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Percentage of students", tickformat = ".0%"),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Academic performance"))
  ) %>%
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, scrollZoom = FALSE)


#running statistical test
presentation_academic %>%
  {
    table(
      droplevels(.$LikePresentation),
      droplevels(.$AcademicPerformance)
    )
  } %>%
  fisher.test() %>%
  {
    tibble(
      test = "Fisher's exact test",
      n = nrow(presentation_academic),
      p = .$p.value
    )
  } %>%
  mutate(p = if_else(p < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Association between presentation preference and academic performance",
    col.names = c("Test", "Students", "p-value"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
```

The stacked bar chart shows that students who liked giving presentations generally reported higher academic performance. Around 55% of this group reported Good or Excellent performance, compared with 40% of those who did not like presentations. Below Average performance occurred only among students who disliked presentations (13.3%), while Excellent performance occurred only among those who liked them (approximately 13%).

Among the 99 students analysed, Fisher’s exact test indicated a statistically significant association between presentation preference and academic performance (p = .004). This provides evidence that the performance distributions differed between the two groups, providing support for our hypotheses. Considering the descriptive data in the graph, this association is likely positive. However, although the chart suggests more favourable performance among students who liked presentations, the test does not establish that liking presentations causes better academic performance.

### Liking new things

```{r}
#preparing data
new_things_academic <- presentation_academic %>%
  mutate(LikeNewThings = factor(LikeNewThings, levels = c("No", "Yes")))

#plotting
new_things_academic %>%
  count(LikeNewThings, AcademicPerformance) %>%
  group_by(LikeNewThings) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n),
    hover = str_c(
      "Likes new things: ", LikeNewThings,
      "<br>Academic performance: ", AcademicPerformance,
      "<br>Students: ", n, " of ", sum(n),
      "<br>Percentage: ", scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  plot_ly(
    x = ~LikeNewThings, y = ~proportion,
    color = ~AcademicPerformance,
    colors = viridisLite::viridis(4),
    type = "bar", text = ~hover, hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Academic performance by preference for new things",
    barmode = "stack",
    xaxis = list(title = "Likes new things"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Percentage of students", tickformat = ".0%"),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Academic performance"))
  ) %>%
  config(displaylogo = FALSE, scrollZoom = FALSE)

#running statistical test and putting it into a nice table
new_things_academic %>%
  {
    table(
      droplevels(.$LikeNewThings),
      droplevels(.$AcademicPerformance)
    )
  } %>%
  fisher.test() %>%
  {
    tibble(
      test = "Fisher's exact test",
      n = nrow(new_things_academic),
      p = .$p.value
    )
  } %>%
  mutate(p = if_else(p < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Association between liking new things and academic performance",
    col.names = c("Test", "Students", "p-value"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
```

The stacked bar chart shows that students who did not like new things reported either Average (40%) or Good (60%) academic performance. Among those who liked new things, approximately 46% reported Average performance, 39% Good, 10% Excellent, and 4.5% Below Average. Although Excellent performance occurred only among students who liked new things, this group also included all Below Average responses, so the chart does not show a clear pattern of higher performance.

Among the 99 students analysed, Fisher’s exact test found no statistically significant association between liking new things and academic performance (p = .702). The observed differences therefore do not provide clear evidence that academic-performance distributions differ between the two groups. Therefore, disproving our hypothesis and proving the null instead. This does not prove that no relationship exists, particularly given the small number of students who did not like new things.

### Exploratory multivariable modelling

Exploratory ordinal logistic regression was used to assess the associations of friendship count, presentation preference, and preference for new things with academic performance jointly. A logarithmic transformation of friendship count improved model fit, but diagnostic tests suggested violations of the proportional-odds assumption. A partial proportional-odds model had a lower AIC but produced extreme coefficients and unavailable standard errors, consistent with separation arising from sparse outcome–preference combinations. Therefore, adjusted effects were not interpreted, code output is below for reference.

```{r}
# 1. Use the same complete-case sample for all models
model_variables <- c(
  "AcademicPerformance", "NumberOfFriend",
  "LikePresentation", "LikeNewThings"
)

model_data <- academic_data[
  complete.cases(academic_data[, model_variables]),
  model_variables
]

# Explicitly set the correct outcome order
model_data$AcademicPerformance <- ordered(
  model_data$AcademicPerformance,
  levels = c("Below Average", "Average", "Good", "Excellent")
)

# 2. Compare original and log-transformed friendship counts
model <- ordinal::clm(
  AcademicPerformance ~ NumberOfFriend + LikePresentation + LikeNewThings,
  data = model_data,
  link = "logit"
)

model_log <- ordinal::clm(
  AcademicPerformance ~ log1p(NumberOfFriend) +
    LikePresentation + LikeNewThings,
  data = model_data,
  link = "logit"
)


knitr::kable(
  AIC(model, model_log),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Comparison of friendship-count specifications",
  col.names = c("Estimated parameters", "AIC")
)

# 3. Check proportional odds for the log model
ordinal::nominal_test(model_log)

# 4. Fit and assess the partial proportional-odds model
model_partial <- ordinal::clm(
  AcademicPerformance ~ LikeNewThings,
  nominal = ~ log1p(NumberOfFriend) + LikePresentation,
  data = model_data,
  link = "logit"
)

knitr::kable(
  AIC(model_log, model_partial),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Comparison of proportional-odds and partial proportional-odds models",
  col.names = c("Estimated parameters", "AIC")
)

# 5. Inspect instability and sparse cells (each output printed once)
print(summary(model_partial))

with(model_data, table(AcademicPerformance, LikePresentation))
with(model_data, table(AcademicPerformance, LikeNewThings))
```
:::
